message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for me to take a seat in the front row of my college class, especially since there are designated priority seats for disabled students. Let me start by understanding the situation better. First, the class is MWF, but the first day was last Wednesday because Monday was a holiday. I went to the first day, but it was really crowded, so I had to stand in the back. Then I missed the Friday and Monday lectures. Today, Wednesday, was my first day back. I knew the class was going to be packed again, so I came 10 minutes early to get a seat in the front row. I have anxiety, and sitting in the front helps me feel more comfortable asking and answering questions without shouting across the room. I can do well in the class even if I have to sit in the back, but sitting in the front is a strong preference for me. All seats are first come, first served. There are two priority seats specifically designated for disabled students. These seats are only open to able-bodied students when they're unoccupied. To use these priority seats, you have to notify the school, and then the professor makes sure the seat is available to you every lecture. For the other seats, after a few weeks, people tend to sit in the same spots, giving the impression that it's their "seat" for the rest of the semester, even though it's technically not assigned. When I sat down today, I noticed two girls walking in together, talking and laughing. One girl sat behind me, and the other stood next to me and said, "Hi, sorry, actually you're sitting in my seat." I responded by saying there's no assigned seating; anyone can sit anywhere. She replied, "Yeah, but I've been sitting in this seat all semester (this is our 3rd lecture out of like 30)." She mentioned there are still open seats in the back that I could move to. I countered by saying that if there are open seats in the back for me, there are also open seats in the back for her. She then said, "Look...I'm deaf in one ear. I need a seat in the front row. Move please," and I noticed her hearing aid. I pointed out that if she needed a front seat because of her hearing issue, she should be registered with the disabled students department to ensure she has priority seating. This isn't a priority seat, I said. She responded, "I don't need to register anything with the school and I don't need to explain myself to you. It's my seat...I told you I need it because I'm hard of hearing." I replied, "Wouldn't those same rules apply to me as well? Not needing to explain myself to you?" Girl 2 then said, "Stop being an asshole and just fucking move...jesus." I said, "I'm done talking. I'm not moving." Girl 1 and Girl 2 scoffed, and Girl 1 found another seat. I don't feel like I did anything wrong, but I spent the rest of the class overhearing everyone behind me talking shit about me. It's important to note that we're always given worksheets that we can work on with the person behind us, so it's possible Girl 1 mostly wanted my seat so she could work with Girl 2 on it. Also, I was in the front seat in the far left corner. There are about 10 seats closer to the middle board than the seat I was in. So, is it right or wrong for me to take that seat? Let me think through this step by step. First, the priority seats are specifically for disabled students. I'm not disabled, so I shouldn't be using those seats unless they're unoccupied. In this case, the seat I took wasn't a priority seat; it was a regular seat. So, in that sense, I wasn't taking a seat that was reserved for someone else. However, the girls were insistent that it was "their" seat, even though technically, all seats are first come, first served. They had been sitting there for a few weeks, but that doesn't make it their assigned seat. I came early to secure a seat in the front because of my anxiety, which is a valid reason for wanting to sit there. Girl 1 mentioned she's deaf in one ear and needs a front seat. That sounds like a legitimate need, but she wasn't using a priority seat. If she needed a front seat due to her disability, she should have registered with the disabled students department to ensure she gets priority seating. Since she didn't, she was just like any other student trying to secure a seat. Girl 2 was more confrontational, telling me to move. I stood my ground because I felt I had the right to sit there since it wasn't a priority seat, and I came early to get a front seat for my anxiety. The fact that I overheard people talking negatively about me afterward is unfortunate, but I don't think that changes whether my action was right or wrong. I was just trying to sit where I felt comfortable and where I could participate better in class. Also, considering that there are about 10 seats closer to the middle board than the one I was in, it seems like there were plenty of other seats available for Girl 1 and Girl 2 to sit together if that was their main concern. In conclusion, I think my decision to sit in that front seat wasn't wrong because it wasn't a priority seat, and I came early to secure a spot due to my anxiety. The other students' insistence that it was "their" seat, despite the first come, first served policy, doesn't make their claim stronger. However, I could have handled the confrontation more gracefully to avoid conflict, but that doesn't make my initial action wrong.
